author: Lucas_Malor

text:
The right primitive here is HKDF (RFC 5869), not PBKDF2 with a counter.
PBKDF2 is for stretching low-entropy passwords. You already have 256 bits of entropy, so the work factor buys you nothing and only makes derivation slow. HKDF exists exactly for deriving many independent keys from one master key, with domain separation via info
python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF

def derive(master: bytes, purpose: str, nonce: int, length: int = 32) -> bytes:
    info = b"secret:v1:" + purpose.encode() + b":" + nonce.to_bytes(8, "big")
    return HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=length, salt=None, info=info).derive(master)
```

Different `info` values yield independent keys, so the nonce is just part of the context and the same derived key is never reused. Keep the master in memory only, mlock it if swap is in your threat model, and never log derived outputs. pbkdf2_hmac with a per-secret salt is still cryptographically fine, but it is the wrong tool: slow by design and easy to misuse.

author: Kenny_6587

text: Your nonce is not guaranteed to be used once: You are relying on filesystem IO and OS state to ensure the program never uses the same nonce. If the file doesn’t write for whatever reason and you run the program again, the nonce will be re-used. Your nonce should not be persisted to storage.

author: Kenny_6587

text:
Because you can’t guarantee that anything read from storage has not been read before. There is no real way to guarantee that you don’t re-use a nonce here. The user might restore from a backup, or the filesystem might lie to you about data being written successfully. Even if you ran things entirely using memory you would still be vulnerable to users using things like VM snapshots which would roll back the nonce.
You simply can’t guarantee that the key you’re using has not signed a value using this nonce before.

author: will_f

text:
As a disclaimer: I am not a cryptographer, so take this with a grain of salt.
I had a bit more of a think about this. To my understanding Kenny wants a deterministic password generator that gives an infinite list of passwords. To avoid re-use it tracks the latest element taken from the list in some way.
The algorithm in the original post is roughly:

Set nonce to 0 at initialization
Import a ‘long term’ seed (we’ll assume it’s a 256-bit seed)
Import a ‘one time’ seed that can be added to (we’ll assume it’s at least a 256-bit seed)
When it’s time to generate a new key, remove and keep 10 characters off the ‘one time’ seed, saving the rest to a file
Increment nonce
Create the plaintext of nonce + the 10 characters one time seed + the 256 bit long term seed
Use PBKDF2 to hash the combination multiple times, skip salting so it’s probably just as strong as multiple sha256 hashes
Save the updated nonce and seed for next time

The author said to ignore the on time seed so we basically have this:

Set nonce to 0
Set seed to some 256-bit value
When it’s time to generate a new key, PBKDF2 the nonce and seed together
Increment the nonce and save it to file

(We can think of the one time seed as just a nonce that changes each time too)
Security-wise there shouldn’t be any way to get the value of sent to the hasher back. If the nonce is re-used it isn’t too much of a problem here specifically because it’s not used to encrypt ciphertext. I’m not sure you would need a key stretching algorithm like PBKDF2 here.
Looking at the HKDF expand mentioned earlier it works by doing multiple iterations to get multiple keys, where each new key is a HMAC digest of your seed, the previous HMAC digest, and the key number. Using a HMAC avoids some attacks that would let attackers without knowing your seed produce an hash for another message (such as a nonce), but I’m not sure how much this matters in your threat model.
But regarding the strength of this mode, the HKDF paper is a good read, specifically section 8 (page 21): https://eprint.iacr.org/2010/264.pdf It goes in to how a ‘traditional’ KDF like your design has to get more bits out of a secret key, how the inputs are highly correlated, and so on.
Mixing in a per-generation salt would be good but require you to store more data. And I’m assuming that’s the problem here: You don’t want to store a bunch of random data, otherwise you wouldn’t want a seed with deterministic output.
But that’s also the problem with this setup: You are not guaranteed to generate a unique secret each time, you may get a secret that has already existed. Now, re-using output secrets here won’t leak your key or let you see other secrets. It just means you’re re-using secrets which in general is a bad idea. Is this a problem for you? It may not be. Finding out a way to avoid this means you need to be more manual about generating a keys, perhaps by tagging the key with something like a website name. At that point you’re mixing a secret with some low-entropy data to get an output, and this is fairly common.
But the downside to this approach of using a deterministic seed is that if the seed is compromised, all of your derived secrets are compromised too. But I’m sure you have already thought of that part of it.



 Will Fatherley:

Asking for forgiveness because it might not be my place to help solve the problem, but I’m wondering if HKDF itself might be a useful tool to generate a nonce at each run of main since it is designed to output >=1 secure keys (return one to the user, save another to JSON as nonce). This approach doesn’t solve the VM snapshot complication as far as I can tell, but I am not sure a single device could based on the discussion so far.

The only thing I could think that would help there is having the user supply some extra data like mentioned above, or using the clock as input somehow. But too fine a clock input makes the space for generated secrets huge and too coarse means they could still accidentally overlap.

There are two important differences between PBKDF2 and just SHA256, that I am aware of (so their might be more)

PBKDF2 is side channel attack resistant and SHA256 is not.

The SHA256 and PBKDF2 functions are not guaranteed to be constant time, see the documentation for lack of guarantee. For actually comparing hashes constant time can be important somewhat, but you’re not comparing any hashes here. If you were you would want to use a function marked as being constant time.

There’s a world of discussion about whether specific code is ‘secure’. You haven’t specified a threat model or even whether it needs to be deterministic (time is now allowed? why not just use random data?), how you plan to keep it secure when things change, or argued why it is secure. You will need to do this with any security code, and the easiest way to make something that is boring and obviously correct.
If I were to start anew, here is what I would give as my solution:
import os
import hashlib
# generates 10 unique passwords from a single seed
salt = os.urandom(16) # can store, may be public
entropy = os.urandom(16) # can store
iters = 10_000_000 # takes around a second or two on my machine
for i in range(0, 10):
  password = entropy + str(i).encode('utf-8')
  key = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', password, salt, iters)
  print(f"new key! {key.hex()}")

So is this secure against a threat model where someone just just the key and wants to get your entropy? I would argue ‘yes’ for the following reasons:

This is a key-derivation function, so we get a key out of it
PBKDF2’s job is make it infeasible to find the input key
We are followingpbkdf2_hmac’s documentation and recommendations
I am delivering the keys to the user as separate keys that they won’t accidentally re-use them

You could use something else, but you now have to write a much longer explanation as to why this is safe, including all the reasons you have strayed from the mainstream path and why the reasons don’t apply to your use case.
For your use case the only reason I can see to not use PBKDF2 is for two reasons. The first is the key stretching is unnecessary when you have a secure key. To that I say the key stretching will do nothing but make things better, not worse. You’re paying a small tax on having something people can agree on is secure.
The second is that you want to learn (I’m assuming that is what this thread is about) and that’s fine. But you have to understand what existing tools do and why first, then you can use that to justify that you don’t need those properties.

If we’re still on the topic of learning, if what we want is a way to:

Mix a key with some insecure, possibly known data
Get a result as secure and unpredictable as the key, and unique to the data

Then any cryptographically secure hash would do.

Say you have a function like this:
def check_password(password):

If I can measure how long check_password(my_input) takes, I can see that it’s slower the more letters at the start match. The short answer is that today with the knowledge and technology we have? No, and breaking the key is infeasible even if each check was instant, the key is simply too long.
The longer answer is that sometimes things get broken and you need to be prepared for that happening. Your 256-bit key might end up being only as strong as 250-bits or 128-bits somehow. It would be a good idea to use PBKDF2 to stretch your key strength up as high as possible so when the day comes that your hash function is weakened it will still take too long to crack a lower security key.

I’m actually going to double back here and explain a bit more why this is the case. Most problems with writing correct code can be solved by looking at documentation of the things we use, other code and arguing that things fit together nicely or poorly.
Security is not one of those things because it heavily relies on the capabilities of the outside world which change day to day. This is why you need to have somebody with knowledge about what is secure now and what might not be secure tomorrow to tell you how long your code will probably be secure for.
